items.note: The whole answer clause is left in English ('They physically change liquid milk mixtures ngadto sa solid frozen treats gamit ang low temperatures'), so the Cebuano itself never states the liquid-to-solid physical change; the question also asks 'Unsay pamaon' (pamaon = bait) instead of the process/method, so a Cebuano-only reader cannot answer from the Cebuano text

title_bis 'Toxoplasma sa Iha sa Iro' names the DOG (iro); English and body are about stray CAT droppings (iring). Body never corrects the title, so a child can come away believing dog waste carries Toxoplasma — a false health claim, and the cat-specificity is the whole point of the card. ('iha' is also not a word here; 'ihi'=urine vs body's 'tae'=feces.)

EN: brain triggers SWEATING to cool the body. BIS: 'nag-trigger og pagpanghupaw' = triggers SIGHING. Never corrected anywhere on the card, and it is the emphasised term. Same batch (ffct-36068) uses 'mopawis' correctly for sweating, so the corpus word exists. A child reads that the brain makes you sigh to cool down = false.

'Kung moluoy ang magma' = 'when the magma takes pity'; the cooling trigger for crystallization is gone and never restored anywhere in the card, so a Cebuano-only child cannot say what makes magma crystallize. Corpus elsewhere correctly uses mobugnaw/nagbugnaw for magma cooling (ffct-15497, ffct-34081)

Cebuano 'bulong' means medicine/remedy (whisper is 'hunghong'); the body reads 'a shout reaches farther than medicine', so the shout-vs-whisper contrast the whole amplitude lesson rests on is never delivered. Only the garbled English title 'Whispir' hints at it

EN asks why we feel weak WITH A FEVER; the Cebuano question asks 'Ngano nga maghuyang ta kung tugnaw?' = when we are COLD, and the answer never mentions hilanat. A child reading the Cebuano learns the wrong trigger (cold weather instead of fever). Only the title carries 'Hilanat', which the body then contradicts. 'tugnaw' is cold, never fever, so the pair is reusable for grep.

EN: a young Brahminy kite is "mostly brown all over". BIS: "Halos tanan kapaw ang batan-on nga Brahminy kite" — kapaw means surface / to come to the surface in Cebuano, never the colour brown (brown = tabunon / kape / kapehon; confirmed against binisaya.com). No other part of the card restores the colour, so a Cebuano-only reader cannot say what a young kite looks like.

EN 'roasted' became 'gilanggaw' (langgaw = vinegar / soured), a different process; the card never says the beans are roasted, so a Cebuano-only reader learns seeds are vinegared then ground. Corpus standard for roasting coffee is 'gisanlag' (ffct-04871, ffct-07532); 'langgaw' occurs only here.

'beak' rendered as 'sungkad' (a pole used to knock fruit down), not a bird part; the card never says 'tuka'/'sungo', so the whole point — finch BEAK shapes vary with food — is unrecoverable. Corpus uses 'tuka' for the same Darwin fact in ffct-02145; 'sungkad' occurs only here.

English: 'Root crops like carrots absorb minerals from soil'. Cebuano: 'Ang root crops like carrots mopasok og minerals sa yuta'. 'Mopasok' means to insert/drive into, not to absorb (mosuyop/mosipsip), so the Cebuano reads as carrots PUTTING minerals INTO the soil — the uptake relationship is reversed and nothing later in the card restores it. A child reading only the Cebuano is left with a false direction for how root crops get minerals. (The scrub-and-peel instruction itself is intact; the reversed clause is the card's reason-giving fact.)

'timailhan sa muabot nga bagyo' turns 'impending thunderstorm' into an incoming typhoon. Bagyo means typhoon/tropical cyclone to Filipino children; the card never corrects it, so a child learns that hot-afternoon cumulonimbus over Manila signals a typhoon. Thunderstorm should be unos / dalugdog-kilat.

Direction reversed: EN 'the sunlight you see now left the Sun eight minutes ago' becomes 'miadto na sa adlaw' = the light WENT TO the sun eight minutes ago. Should be 'mibiya/migikan sa adlaw'. Nothing else in the card states the Sun-to-Earth direction, so a Cebuano-only reader can take away that light travels toward the Sun.

EN: heavy metals POISON root crops like sweet potato (food becomes unsafe). BIS: 'makapamamatay sa mga gamot sa kamote' = kills the kamote's roots. Different consequence, nothing in the card restores the 'contaminated crop is poisonous to eat' fact — the child learns the plant dies, not that the food is unsafe.

EN: glaucoma 'can cause blindness'. BIS uses 'pagkabulag' - Tagalog false friend: in Cebuano 'bulag' means to separate/part, blind is 'buta' (the corpus uses 'makapabuta' correctly in ffct-34730). Nothing else on the card names the outcome, so the Cebuano-only reader never learns glaucoma can blind you - the one fact that motivates the check-up advice.
